html:
Aadhaar, "foundation", is India's identity number: twelve digits tied to a person's fingerprints, iris scans and photograph. Begun in 2009, it covers more than 1.3 billion people and is the largest biometric system in the world.

Hundreds of millions of Indians had no paper that proved who they were: no birth certificate, no fixed address. Without one they could not open a bank account, and subsidies meant for them were stolen through lists of invented names.

The government set up an authority in January 2009 and asked Nandan Nilekani, a founder of Infosys, to run it. The first number was given on 29 September 2010 to Ranjana Sonawane, a woman of a tribal village in Maharashtra. A billion people had enrolled by 2016.

A fingerprint on a small scanner now proves identity anywhere. On this base India built cheap bank accounts, direct payment of pensions and subsidies, and instant mobile payments (see UPI).

The problems are real. Old people and labourers whose fingerprints fail to scan have been refused food rations. Data has leaked. Critics fear a tool for tracking citizens. In 2017 the Supreme Court ruled that privacy is a basic right. In 2018 it upheld Aadhaar for state benefits and taxes and barred companies from demanding it.
sum: Aadhaar, "foundation", is India's identity number: twelve digits tied to a person's fingerprints, iris scans and photograph. Begun in 2009, it covers more than 1.3 billion people and is the largest biometric system in the world.
